pharm: Synthetic fluorinated glucocorticoid; medium-potency topical corticosteroid with anti-inflammatory, antipruritic, and vasoconstrictive actions
quick: Apply thin film to affected area 2-4 times daily (0.025%); 2-3 times daily (0.1%, 0.5%)
Category C; use only if benefit justifies risk, not extensively/prolonged
Use with caution in nursing women
Local skin reactions; HPA-axis suppression if large area/occlusion/prolonged use
summary: Triamcinolone acetonide is a synthetic medium-potency topical corticosteroid used to relieve the inflammatory and pruritic manifestations of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses. It is applied as a thin film to the affected area. Systemic absorption is increased by application to large surface areas, prolonged use, and occlusive dressings, which can cause reversible HPA-axis suppression, Cushing's syndrome, and hyperglycemia, especially in children. It is for external use only and should be used at the least amount compatible with an effective therapeutic regimen.
indications: Relief of the inflammatory and pruritic manifestations of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses

admin: For external use only; apply as a thin film to the affected area and avoid contact with the eyes
Do not bandage, cover, or wrap the treated area occlusively unless directed by the physician
Avoid use on the face, groin, or axillae for prolonged periods and over large surface areas
Discontinue occlusive dressings and institute antimicrobial therapy if infection develops
In children treated in the diaper area, avoid tight-fitting diapers or plastic pants (these act as occlusive dressings)
Use the least amount compatible with an effective therapeutic regimen
moa: Topical corticosteroids share anti-inflammatory, antipruritic, and vasoconstrictive actions. The precise mechanism of anti-inflammatory activity is unclear. Once absorbed through the skin, triamcinolone acetonide is handled through pharmacokinetic pathways similar to systemically administered corticosteroids.

absolute: History of hypersensitivity to triamcinolone acetonide or any component of the preparation
relative: Application to large surface areas, for prolonged periods, or under occlusion (augments systemic absorption)
Dermatological infections without concurrent antimicrobial therapy
Use in pediatric patients (greater susceptibility to HPA-axis suppression and growth effects)
Pregnancy (avoid extensive, large-amount, or prolonged use)
monitor: Local adverse reactions, especially under occlusive dressings
Signs of HPA-axis suppression with large-dose, large-area, or occlusive use (urinary free cortisol, ACTH stimulation tests)
In children: linear growth, weight gain, signs of intracranial hypertension

preg: Pregnancy Category C. Corticosteroids are generally teratogenic in laboratory animals when administered systemically at relatively low doses, and the more potent corticosteroids are teratogenic after dermal application in animals. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Topical corticosteroids should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus, and drugs of this class should not be used extensively, in large amounts, or for prolonged periods on pregnant patients.
lact: It is not known whether topical administration of corticosteroids could result in sufficient systemic absorption to produce detectable quantities in breast milk. Systemically administered corticosteroids are secreted into breast milk in quantities not likely to harm the infant. Nevertheless, caution should be exercised when topical corticosteroids are administered to a nursing woman.
renal: Not applicable (topical). Absorbed corticosteroid metabolites are excreted by the kidneys, but the label provides no specific renal-impairment dosing for topical use.
hepatic: Not applicable (topical). Absorbed corticosteroids are metabolized primarily in the liver, but the label provides no specific hepatic-impairment dosing for topical use.

interactions.diagnostics: Systemic absorption can produce hyperglycemia and glucosuria; HPA-axis suppression can be detected by urinary free cortisol and ACTH stimulation tests.

serious: Reversible HPA-axis suppression (with large doses, large areas, prolonged use, or occlusion)
Manifestations of Cushing's syndrome, hyperglycemia, and glucosuria from systemic absorption
In children: linear growth retardation, delayed weight gain, intracranial hypertension
emergency: Signs of intracranial hypertension in children (bulging fontanelles, headaches, papilledema)
Symptomatic adrenal insufficiency with steroid withdrawal

monitoring: Local adverse reactions, especially under occlusive dressings
Evidence of HPA-axis suppression in patients on large doses of potent steroid, large surface areas, or occlusion (urinary free cortisol, ACTH stimulation tests)
Therapeutic response - discontinue if no favorable response or if infection is present
In children: linear growth, weight gain, plasma cortisol, and signs of intracranial hypertension
counsel: Use this medication exactly as directed; it is for external use only and avoid contact with the eyes
Do not use for any disorder other than the one for which it was prescribed
Do not bandage, cover, or wrap the treated area so it becomes occlusive unless your physician directs
Report any signs of local adverse reactions, especially under an occlusive dressing
For a child treated in the diaper area, do not use tight-fitting diapers or plastic pants
Tell your clinician if you are pregnant or breastfeeding before prolonged or extensive use
pk: Not specified; percutaneous absorption varies with vehicle, skin integrity, and occlusion
Not specified for topical use; absorbed drug follows systemic corticosteroid kinetics
Dosed 2-4 times daily depending on strength
Store at 20-25 degrees C (68-77 degrees F); avoid excessive heat; protect from freezing
pearls: Systemic absorption is augmented by potent steroids, large surface areas, prolonged use, and occlusive dressings - all of which can cause reversible HPA-axis suppression
Recovery of HPA-axis function is generally prompt and complete after discontinuation; rarely steroid-withdrawal symptoms require supplemental systemic corticosteroids
Children absorb proportionally larger amounts and are more susceptible to systemic toxicity and growth suppression
If infection develops under occlusion, stop the dressing and treat with an appropriate antimicrobial
Use the least amount and shortest course needed; avoid the face, groin, and axillae long-term
missed: If a dose is missed, apply it as soon as remembered. If it is almost time for the next application, skip the missed dose and resume the regular schedule. Do not apply a double amount to make up for a missed dose, and do not apply more frequently or over a larger area than directed.
overdose: Topically applied corticosteroids can be absorbed in sufficient amounts to produce systemic effects, including reversible HPA-axis suppression, Cushing's syndrome, hyperglycemia, and glucosuria. If systemic toxicity or HPA-axis suppression occurs, withdraw the drug, reduce the frequency of application, or substitute a less potent steroid; supportive measures and supplemental systemic corticosteroids may be needed for steroid-withdrawal symptoms. Contact Poison Help (1-800-222-1222).
